displayQuote: The Next Time I Send a Damn Fool for Something, I Go Myself

meta.title: Who really said "The Next Time I Send a Damn Fool for Something, I Go Myself"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Samuel Goldwyn. Quote Investigator credits director Michael Curtiz — and the joke itself was printed in Judge magazine in November 1889.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'The Next Time I Send a Damn Fool for Something, I Go Myself'?
meta.ogDescription: Boller & George and Quote Investigator both hand this one to Michael Curtiz. The gag behind it ran in Judge magazine in 1889.

answer.label: Not Samuel Goldwyn — the line belongs to Michael Curtiz
answer.sourceLine: Quote Investigator ↗ traces the remark to Michael Curtiz, the Hungarian-born director of Casablanca, whose mangled English was a standing joke on the Warner Bros. lot. Columnist Sidney Skolsky printed “The next time I send a damn fool, I go myself” as a Curtiz line in November 1936, and Jack Warner’s 1965 memoir gives the longer wording used here. Boller and George’s They Never Said It ↗ is blunter: “It was the tongue-twisting Hungarian director Michael Curtiz, not Goldwyn, who made this priceless remark.” The joke Curtiz walked into is older than either man’s career.

source.heading: Where the line actually comes from

docMeta.dd: Sheilah Graham, The Hartford Courant, 1 May 1936, p. 19
Jack L. Warner, My First Hundred Years in Hollywood (Random House, 1965), pp. 9–10

source.excerpt: Favorite of all the Curtiz remarks is the one he pulled when an assistant director failed to bring what he had been sent for. Director Curtiz shouted: “The next time I send a damn fool, I go myself.”
trail: 23 November 1889 — the gag appears as invention in the New York humor weekly Judge ↗, in a squib titled “The Easiest Way”: a man called Jones tells a servant, “When I’m tempted to send a fool on an errand again I’ll not ask you—I’ll go myself.” Quote Investigator ↗ has this as the earliest instance; the bound volume is on Google Books ↗.

1 May 1936 — columnist Sheilah Graham ↗ watches Curtiz shoot The Charge of the Light Brigade and quotes him wailing, after a third ruined take, “Next time I send a fool into the charge, I’ll go myself.” QI ↗ calls this the most directly supported version, while noting Curtiz may have spoken more than one.

1936 to 1965 — the wording settles. Sidney Skolsky ↗ prints “The next time I send a damn fool, I go myself” that November; Time lists “Next time I send some fool for something I go myself” among its Curtizisms in August 1940; Jack Warner’s memoir gives the full sentence in 1965 — all per QI ↗.

1969 — Norman Zierold’s The Moguls ↗ singles the quote out to reject it: “Goldwyn definitely did not say, ‘The next time I send a fool for something, I go myself.’ That was Hungarian director Michael Curtiz shouting at a hapless messenger who had brought back the wrong article.” Boller and George ↗ repeat the finding in They Never Said It, pp. 41–42.
source.excerptNote: Skolsky’s version has no “for something” in it. The longer form this page is titled with is the one Jack L. Warner printed in My First Hundred Years in Hollywood (1965), recalling Curtiz “who once broke up a studio conference by shouting” it. Both passages are quoted from Quote Investigator’s transcriptions ↗; the underlying newspapers sit in subscription archives we could not open, so we are relying on QI’s reading of them rather than our own.

source.rightsNote: We assert no rights status for this sentence. The 1889 Judge squib it descends from is long out of copyright, but that is a different wording. The line as quoted here is reported speech whose earliest printings are a 1936 newspaper column and a 1965 memoir — both after the 1931 United States public-domain threshold, and both still notionally protected as texts. Quote it as reportage and attribute it to Curtiz, not to Goldwyn.

author.name: Michael Curtiz
author.heading: The director who actually said it
author.metaLine: 1886–1962 · Hungarian-American film director, Casablanca and Mildred Pierce
author.bio: Born Manó Kaminer in Budapest and known from 1905 as Kertész Mihály, Michael Curtiz had already directed 64 films in Europe when Warner Bros. brought him to Hollywood in 1926. He made 102 more there, among them Casablanca, Mildred Pierce and The Adventures of Robin Hood. His English never caught up with his eye. Time reported in 1940 that Warner jokers hung signs on his sets reading “English Broken Here” and “Curtiz Spoken Here,” and that he was “the butt of more Hollywood stories than Sam Goldwyn” — which is exactly how a joke first printed in 1889 came to be filed under his name, and then under Goldwyn’s.

misattribution.heading: Who has been credited — and who actually said it
misattribution.intro: Search the line today and it comes back as a Goldwynism. Two reference works reassign it to the same other man, and the joke underneath it was in print before either of them had made a film.

items.why: Norman Zierold’s The Moguls (1969) ↗ picks this quote out specifically to deny it — “Goldwyn definitely did not say” it — and Wikiquote ↗ files it under Misattributed, citing Boller and George.

Two Hollywood columnists put a version of the line in his mouth in 1936: Sheilah Graham ↗ on a film set in May, Sidney Skolsky ↗ from a script girl’s shorthand in November. QI ↗ treats Graham’s as the best supported.
The punch line was already a printed gag — “I’ll not ask you—I’ll go myself” — in Judge of 23 November 1889 ↗, per QI ↗. Curtiz reproduced it without knowing it existed.

The twice-decorated Marine gunnery sergeant, himself famous for idiosyncratic English, is credited with “Next time I send a goddam fool, I go myself” in Robert Debs Heinl’s Soldiers of the Sea (1962), per QI ↗. Same joke, third owner.

misattribution.truthLine: The line as quoted is Michael Curtiz’s, reported by two Hollywood columnists in 1936 and repeated by Jack Warner in 1965 — and the joke it is built on was a magazine squib in 1889. Read Quote Investigator’s full chronology ↗.

context.heading: How a magazine gag became a Goldwynism
lead: The remark is a genuine Curtizism ↗, and Curtiz produced them by the dozen: Time counted him “the butt of more Hollywood stories than Sam Goldwyn” in 1940 and reported that colleagues hung “English Broken Here” signs on his sets. What makes this one worth a page is that he was not inventing anything. He was reproducing, out loud and in front of a columnist, a joke a New York humor weekly had printed as fiction in 1889, when Curtiz was a small child in Budapest.

Goldwyn’s part in it is structural rather than personal. By the 1930s he had become the address that unattached Hollywood malapropisms were delivered to. Wikipedia ↗ puts it flatly: “Goldwynisms were the inventions of humorists and newspaper editors,” and many of them “predate Goldwyn’s career.” He came to resent it. Boller and George ↗ quote him giving up on the whole genre: “None of them are true. They’re all made up by a bunch of comedians and pinned on me.”
context.detailsSummary: The 1889 original, and the men it passed through
detailsBody: “The Easiest Way” ran in Judge on 23 November 1889 and is pure fiction: “Jones, having sent a stupid servant to do an errand, was greatly annoyed on finding that he had done exactly the opposite of what he had been ordered. ‘Why, you haven’t common-sense,’ he remonstrated… ‘Shut up! I should have remembered that you were an idiot. When I’m tempted to send a fool on an errand again I’ll not ask you—I’ll go myself.’” Quote Investigator ↗ tracks reprints through the Boston Herald the following day, Judge’s Library in 1891, a Sacramento periodical in 1893, and an Ogdensburg newspaper in 1902 where “Jones” has become “Scones.”

After Curtiz the line kept moving. By 1962 it had reached the United States Marine Corps, where Robert Debs Heinl’s Soldiers of the Sea credited it to gunnery sergeant Louis Cukela in the form “Next time I send a goddam fool, I go myself.” By then the joke had been in print for more than seventy years, under at least four different owners, and the one man who certainly never said it was the one whose name it now carries.
context.pull: Curtiz did not invent the joke. He walked into it, on a film set, in front of a columnist.

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator's earliest instance is a fictional gag in Judge (New York) of 23 November 1889, p. 110 ('The Easiest Way'); Sheilah Graham quoted Curtiz saying 'Next time I send a fool into the charge, I'll go myself' in The Hartford Courant of 1 May 1936, p. 19; Sidney Skolsky printed 'The next time I send a damn fool, I go myself' as Curtiz's in the Augusta Chronicle of 24 November 1936, p. 4; Time of 19 August 1940 listed 'Next time I send some fool for something I go myself' among Curtizisms and called him 'the butt of more Hollywood stories than Sam Goldwyn'; Jack L. Warner's My First Hundred Years in Hollywood (Random House, 1965), pp. 9-10, gives 'The next time I send a damn fool for something, I go myself'; and Norman Zierold's The Moguls (1969), pp. 127-128, states 'Goldwyn definitely did not say' it and assigns it to Curtiz. QI concludes Graham's version 'appears to be the most directly supported'.

Paul F. Boller Jr. and John George, They Never Said It (1989), p. 41-42, prints: 'NEXT-TIME-I-SEND-A-FOOL QUOTE "The next time I send a damn fool for something, I go myself." It was the tongue-twisting Hungarian director Michael Curtiz, not Goldwyn, who made this priceless remark.' The same section (p. 40) records Goldwyn saying of the Goldwynisms, 'None of them are true. They're all made up by a bunch of comedians and pinned on me.'

Wikiquote's Samuel Goldwyn page lists 'The next time I send a damn fool for something, I go myself.' in its Misattributed section, sourced to Paul F. Boller and John George, They Never Said It (1990), p. 41-42.

Wikipedia states Michael Curtiz was born Mano Kaminer, from 1905 Mihaly Kertesz, on December 25, 1886 and died April 10, 1962; that he was a Hungarian and American film director; that he had directed 64 films in Europe before Warner Bros. brought him to Hollywood in 1926; and that he directed 102 films during his Hollywood career.

Wikipedia's Samuel Goldwyn article states that 'Goldwynisms were the inventions of humorists and newspaper editors' and that 'Many famous "Goldwynisms" predate Goldwyn's career as circulated witticism'.

Google Books holds a full-view scan of the bound volume of Judge identified by Quote Investigator as the source of the 23 November 1889 gag (volume identity confirmed: the page title reads "The Judge - Google Books"). The specific page 110 was not independently paged through; the transcription above is QI’s.
Internet Archive holds a catalogue record for Norman Zierold, The Moguls (1969), the book Quote Investigator quotes. The full text is lending-restricted and was not read here.
